Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I feel isolated and set apart from others
I should have protected others and I failed

vignette:
Sameer had been a tax consultant for a decade before he took the sabbatical. He wanted, for once, to do something that felt unequivocally good. The six months with the international relief agency were meant to be that. The end of his tour was just three weeks away when the marketplace was hit. He remembers the sequence in fragments, a deck of cards thrown in the air. There was the loud, calm voice of a local official arguing with a vendor, a flash of anger in his eyes. Then the concussion of the blast, a force that threw him against a wall. He remembers the ground, the grit in his mouth, and curling into a ball with his arms over his head. The smell is what stays with him most-a choking mix of burning plastic, dust, and something else, something acrid and sweet. When he could finally look up, the world was grey smoke and screams. He saw things he doesn't allow himself to fully recall, but the feeling of it is always there: a profound, gut-wrenching certainty that he should have done more, that he was there to help and had instead just hidden on the ground while others died. He believes he failed them.

Returning home to his wife and his quiet suburban life was a jarring dislocation. The world he had known, one governed by rules, logic, and a basic sense of fairness, felt like a distant memory, a story someone else had told him. This new world was menacing and unpredictable. Back in his office, the ordinary sounds of life became threats. A car door slamming in the parking lot would cause him to flinch so violently he'd knock over his coffee. His concentration, once his greatest professional asset, was shattered. He would stare at a client's financial records, the numbers blurring into meaningless shapes, his mind snagged on the image of a child's shoe lying in the rubble. He began making mistakes and had to ask his manager to double-check all his filings, a humiliating admission of his new incompetence. The feeling of failure was compounded when an email arrived from the relief agency. They spoke of rebuilding, of his 'valuable contributions', and floated the idea of him returning for a brief consultation in the same city. Sameer stared at the words, his heart hammering against his ribs. The thought of walking those streets again, of breathing that air, was physically unbearable. He dragged the message to the trash and then permanently deleted it, a small, frantic act of self-preservation that felt, seconds later, like another profound act of cowardice.

The triggers were everywhere. One afternoon, a client grew frustrated, his voice rising in calm but firm anger over a tax liability. Sameer felt the air leave his lungs. He saw not a disgruntled client but the furious official in the market, seconds before the explosion. He had to excuse himself, locking himself in a bathroom stall until the shaking subsided. He started avoiding client meetings, conducting all business over email. The smell of a neighbor's bonfire one evening sent him into a full-blown panic, forcing him to retreat to the basement. When a colleague's father passed away, he couldn't bring himself to attend the funeral; the very thought of being in a place so explicitly dedicated to grief was unbearable.

His life began to shrink. He had come to believe that he didn't deserve happiness, not after what he'd witnessed, not after his failure. He and his wife had planned a trip to celebrate their anniversary, but he cancelled it, telling her he was too busy with work. The truth was, the idea of relaxing on a beach, of feeling hopeful or joyful, felt like a betrayal of those who had lost everything. He felt utterly set apart from everyone, including his wife, as if he were living behind a thick wall of glass. At night, the feeling of threat was most acute. He would lie awake for hours, listening to the house settle, certain that the darkness held some imminent danger. Often, a memory would surface-not as a story, but as a bodily sensation. He would find himself unconsciously tensing, his arms creeping up to shield his head, his body reenacting the posture of terror he held on the dusty ground. Each time, a wave of shame would wash over him, hot and suffocating.

It was his wife who finally broke through the isolation. She found him one night, sitting alone in the dark living room long after she had gone to bed. She didn't speak, but simply sat with him, her presence a quiet question. In that moment, he realized how far he had drifted, not just from his old self, but from the person he loved most. He is seeking help now not because he believes he can be fixed-he is certain some things are permanently broken-but because he is terrified of losing what little he has left. He feels like a ghost in his own life and is holding on to the faint hope that therapy might help him learn how to live in it again.
